title: [Chapitre] IX et IX bis. [Ateliers] : notes manuscrites (05-15/07/1986).

deep.reconstruction:
Context: in Chapter IX ('Ateliers', July 1986) Grothendieck builds combinatorial 'maquettes', which are finite ordered sets of cells with relations ⊴, ≤, ≪, ∥, modelling tamely stratified spaces. Here the space is a one-dimensional interval. The basic object is M(I,∂I), where I is a finite totally ordered set whose extreme elements ω0 < ω1 form the boundary ∂I. Its elements are the points a ∈ I (0-cells) and the intervals I_{a,b}, a < b (1-cells, closed or open). The previous page showed how to remove the endpoint ω0. Set J = I∖{ω0}, which has a largest element ω1. Then M(I,∂I)∖{ω0} can be described intrinsically as M(J,ω1). Its objects are the points a ∈ J, the finite intervals J_{a,b}, and new 'half-infinite' objects J_{<a}. These J_{<a} are the traces of the intervals I_{ω0,a}, which have lost their left endpoint.

This page does three things.
(1) It finishes the degenerate example I = {ω0,ω1}. Then J = {ω1} and M(J,ω1) = {ω1, J_{<ω1}}, a two-element set which is still a maquette (a half-open edge). Grothendieck notes a subtlety: the set-theoretic 'interior' |J_{<ω1}|° is empty, since there are no lattice points strictly below ω1 in J. But the cell J°_{<ω1}, the open half-interval it stands for, is non-empty. So the abstract cell must not be confused with its set of vertices.
(2) 'Traitement no 2' is the mirror case. Remove ω1 and set J = I∖{ω1}, with smallest element ω0. Then M(I,∂I)∖{ω1} = M(J,ω0), and one must introduce the objects J_{>a} (a ∈ J) in addition to the points and the finite intervals J_{a,b}.
(3) Remove both endpoints and set J = I∖∂I. Then M(I,∂I)∖∂I = M(J), and one needs three kinds of new object. These are the J_{<a}, the J_{>a} (traces of I_{ω0,a} and I_{a,ω1}), and a 'unit' object [J] representing the whole open interval I_{ω0,ω1}.

The next page justifies [J]. The singular configurations of a full figure, {J_{<a}, J_{>a}} or {J_{<a}, J_{a,b}, J_{>b}}, require it. It also insists that the case J = ∅ (I = {ω0,ω1}) must not be excluded: the indivisible open interval is represented by the empty ordered set, and the maquette is {[J]}. The next page then unifies all four cases as triples (I, Ω0, Ω1). Here Ω0 and Ω1 are subsets of I consisting of a smallest (resp. largest) element, so each has cardinality ≤ 1, and they are disjoint. The four cases are closed, the two half-open, and open intervals.

Purpose: an intrinsic combinatorial description of the cell posets of subdivided closed, half-open and open intervals. These serve as the one-dimensional building blocks of the 'maquettes' (combinatorial models of tame stratified spaces / tame topology) of this chapter.
errors: No mathematical error. The only delicate point is the notation |J_{<ω1}|° = ∅ versus J°_{<ω1} ≠ ∅. Grothendieck flags it himself: the vertex set of the abstract cell is empty while the cell itself, the open half-interval, is non-empty.

Minor inconsistency in the drafting of the examples. In the first case one keeps the largest element ω1 inside J and only adds J_{<a}. In the open case a separate unit object [J] must be added because the interval spanning both missing endpoints has no vertex left. This is consistent, but the asymmetry is only made explicit on the next page.

ideas.what: Combinatorial model (poset of cells with incidence relations) of a subdivided interval, and of what remains after deleting boundary points; deletion is expressed intrinsically in terms of the remaining ordered set J.
ideas.modern_name: Face/cell poset of a 1-dimensional stratified space; exit-path or entrance-path poset of a stratified interval
ideas.usually_credited_to: Classical (cell complexes); stratified versions by MacPherson, Treumann, Lurie, Ayala–Francis–Tanaka (2000s–2010s)
ideas.where_published: Only in spirit: the Esquisse d'un programme §5 (tame topology, 'dévissage' of stratified structures) gives the programme but not this combinatorics.

ideas.what: Half-infinite cells J_{<a}, J_{>a} and a unit cell [J] to model half-open and open intervals; the open indivisible interval is represented by the empty ordered set (next page).
ideas.modern_name: Open interval as empty linear order / augmented simplex category; Joyal duality between finite linear orders and finite bipointed intervals
ideas.usually_credited_to: Joyal (duality Δ ↔ intervals, c. 1997); standard in augmented simplicial combinatorics

ideas.what: Unified data (I, Ω0, Ω1): Ω0, Ω1 are disjoint subsets consisting of at most a minimal (resp. maximal) element, giving four interval types.
ideas.modern_name: Linear orders with optional endpoints / bipointed vs. partially pointed intervals

missed.claim: Grothendieck explicitly encodes the open, half-open and closed intervals by an ordered set J plus optional endpoint data, with the open indivisible interval corresponding to J = ∅. This is essentially the interval/ordinal duality later made standard by Joyal and used in exit-path combinatorics of stratified spaces. It is an early instance in Grothendieck's tame-topology programme, apparently not noticed in the literature on his 'maquettes'.
missed.quote: un objet unité [J] qui figure bien sûr I_{ω0,ω1}
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This is of minor historical interest: it documents that Grothendieck's 1986 combinatorial approach to tame stratified spaces anticipated now-standard conventions (empty poset ↔ open edge) used in combinatorial models of stratified spaces and ∞-categories of exit paths.

deep.surprise_reason: This is careful but elementary bookkeeping for cell posets of subdivided intervals with some endpoints removed. Its interest is mainly as a detail of the unpublished 'maquettes' programme for tame topology, with a mild foreshadowing of Joyal-type interval/ordinal conventions.
transcription_corrections: Line 2: 'morphisme[?] qui consiste en deux éléments seulement' should read 'un ensemble qui consiste en deux éléments seulement'.
'ω0 est dernier[?] en [-tant-] que plus petit élément' is more likely 'ω0 est donné en tant que plus petit élément'.

'Prenons enfin le cas des morphismes[?] voisinant[?] de ∂I dans M' is more likely 'Prenons enfin le cas de l'ensemble résiduel de ∂I dans M', i.e. the complement of ∂I. This matches the previous page's 'ensemble résiduel'.
The word transcribed '"lisses" a, b' is uncertain; it may be '"points"' (the 0-cells a, b) and should be checked against the image.

The left-margin addition near '(a ∈ J)' is barely legible. It seems to say something like 'mais, s'ils sont singuliers, c'est maintenant dans J !' The current transcription '...si singulier, c'est franchement[?] dans J !' is doubtful.
'[-pour-] les "traces"': the crossed-out word looks like 'pour' over the start of an insertion; reading 'pour les "traces" des intervalles I_{ω0,a}, I_{a,ω1}' is fine.
